newsitem.title: FRANCE: French Renault unions warn of long fight.
newsitem.headline: French Renault unions warn of long fight.

text.p: Trade union leaders at French car maker Renault SA warned the management on Tuesday it could face a long labour conflict over bitterly contested plans to close down a factory in Belgium and cut staff in France.

A senior French government parliamentarian meanwhile urged Renault chairman Louis Schweitzer to open negotiations with the workforce and the government on an early retirement plan rejected by the industry ministry last week.

Michel Pericard, National Assembly floor leader of President Jacques Chirac's Gaullist RPR party, told RTL radio he was sure the government had not said its last word and would reconsider the plan to shed 40,000 older workers if it was sure it would lead to the recruitment of young job-seekers.

Union leaders complained they had been neither consulted nor informed about Renault's sudden announcement last Thursday that it was closing its plant in Vilvoorde, near Brussels, the home town of Belgian Prime Minister Jean-Luc Dehaene, with the loss of 3,100 jobs.

There have since been media reports, not officially confirmed by the company, that Renault, whose sales in France slumped by 24 percent in January, also plans to shed about 3,000 jobs in France this year.
Daniel Richter of the pro-Socialist CFDT union said a call for a one-hour strike on Friday at Renault plants in France, Belgium and Spain to protest at the closure was only the start.
"We hope this is the beginning of a long period of labour struggle at Renault all over Europe," he told Europe 1 radio.
"This is an unacceptable method and has produced entirely justified reactions. It is unworthy of Renault," said Philippe Martinez, an official of the communist-led CGT union, the largest at Renault.
"It's obviously just the start of a mobilisation against job cuts," he said.
The Flanders regional government has said it will sue Renault for allegedly failing to inform and consult staff before announcing the closure of Vilvoorde.
